nameStory: The marsh pea gets its straightforward name from its preference for wet, marshy places and its membership in the pea family. Like its garden pea cousins, it produces the characteristic pea-like flowers and pods that legumes are famous for. The scientific name 'palustris' comes from the Latin word for 'swamp,' doubly emphasizing this plant's love of soggy ground.
description: Marsh pea is a climbing perennial wildflower that scrambles through wetland vegetation using curly tendrils like a natural grappling hook. This delicate-looking plant produces clusters of 2-8 pinkish-purple pea flowers, each about the size of a dime. The leaves are made up of oval leaflets arranged in pairs, giving the whole plant a neat, organized appearance. It's a relatively uncommon find in New England, making any discovery feel special.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic pea-shaped flowers in soft pinkish-purple hues, clustered in groups of 2-8 on a single stem. Each flower is roughly 2 centimeters wide with the distinctive 'banner and wings' shape that looks like a tiny butterfly perched on the stem.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 2-6 oval or oblong leaflets arranged in pairs along the stem. The leaflets feel smooth and thin, about the length of your thumbnail, with a fresh, slightly sweet scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A climbing vine that uses branched, coiled tendrils to grab onto nearby plants for support. The tendrils feel springy and curl tightly around anything they touch, like tiny corkscrews.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces typical legume pods that split open when ripe to release round peas inside. The pods are smooth to the touch and make a subtle rattling sound when mature seeds are shaken inside.

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Always found in wet areas - if your feet aren't getting damp or you're not near water, you're probably not looking at marsh pea. This plant is a reliable indicator of consistently moist soil.

habitat: Marsh pea thrives in wetlands, soggy meadows, stream edges, and marshy areas throughout New England. Look for it in places where the soil stays consistently moist or even waterlogged, often growing alongside sedges, cattails, and other moisture-loving plants. It's particularly fond of areas that flood seasonally but aren't permanently underwater.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, with fresh green compound leaves unfurling and tendrils beginning their search for support structures.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time brings the characteristic pinkish-purple pea flowers, making this the best season for positive identification. Flowers gradually develop into green seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open to release peas, while leaves begin to yellow. The plant starts to die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the perennial root system alive underground until spring returns.

funFact: Despite being in the pea family and producing pea-like seeds, marsh pea and many of its wild relatives can be toxic to both humans and livestock if eaten in large quantities - so resist the urge to snack on these 'wild peas' even though they look temptingly similar to edible garden varieties!
confusionNotes: Marsh pea can be confused with other wild members of the pea family, but its wetland habitat is a dead giveaway - most other wild peas prefer drier ground. The pinkish-purple flowers and consistently wet habitat combination is your best identification duo. Remember: 'pink peas need wet feet' to distinguish it from the yellow-flowered meadow pea or the beach-loving seaside pea.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'wild pea' can be confusing since many plants in this family look similar but have very different edibility and safety profiles. Always treat wild peas as potentially toxic - even though they're related to garden peas, evolution has given many wild species chemical defenses that make them unsuitable for human consumption.
compareHints: Among its Lathyrus relatives, marsh pea is distinguished by its wetland habitat and pinkish-purple flowers. Seaside pea grows on beaches with larger purple flowers, meadow pea prefers dry areas with bright yellow blooms, and the escaped garden varieties like broad-leaved sweet pea are typically found near old homesteads rather than in wild marshes. If you're standing in a swamp looking at pink pea flowers, you've likely found the genuine marsh pea.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Lathyrus species, seaside pea is the only one with those distinctive thick, waxy blue-green leaves and strict beach habitat.
Among New England's sweet peas, broad-leaved sweet pea stands out with its distinctly wide leaflets - most others like meadow pea have narrow, grass-like leaflets.
Among New England's wild peas, narrow-leaved everlasting-pea stands out with its bold pink flowers and strongly winged stems.
Among New England's wild peas, meadow pea stands out with its bright yellow flowers - most of its relatives like seaside pea and marsh pea have purple or pink blooms.

Unlike the broad-leaved sweet pea which has wider leaflets and no tubers, or the seaside pea which has 6-12 leaflets, tuberous pea is distinguished by its simple two-leaflet arrangement and underground tuber system.
Unlike its Lathyrus relatives in New England, spring vetch lacks the climbing tendrils found on species like broad-leaved sweet pea and narrow-leaved everlasting-pea.
Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, sweet pea stands out for its incredible fragrance and annual growth habit.

Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, pale vetchling stands out for its uniquely subdued flower color – while seaside pea has purple flowers, meadow pea is bright yellow, and broad-leaved sweet pea shows off in magenta.
Grass pea stands out from its New England Lathyrus cousins primarily by its unique brick-red flowers - no other sweet pea or vetchling in our region shares this color.
